Now, U.S. officials fret Beijing’s spies have orchestrated a major coup: ensnaring now-former Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, one of the most high-profile players behind the AI boom.

   • Democratic senators have told Elon Musk to preserve all records related to SpaceX’s restrictions on Ukraine’s use of its Starlink and Starshield satellite services. 

   • The White House ordered federal officials to approve the release of tens of millions of dollars’ worth of detained illegal Chinese vapes into the U.S. market after conversations with Trump administration political adviser Chris LaCivita and his son.

   • Microsoft’s 19-hour global email outage was the workplace equivalent of a snow day . Some users were frustrated. Some simply checked out from work. The tech giant said it had restored full service early Saturday.

   • The Trump administration said states can delay until July the full implementation of Medicaid work requirements. 

   • An international health body revoked the U.S.’s measles elimination status , a stunning reversal for a nation that had kept the vaccine-preventable disease at bay for decades.

       3. FROM THE MARKETS   • Shares of Nvidia closed the week down 13%. Despite the selloff extending to other chip makers Friday , the PHLX Semiconductor index, which includes Nvidia rivals such as AMD and Broadcom, logged a weekly gain of 8%.

READ IT HERE FIRST   Inside Stephen Miller’s frenetic first week as White House chief of staff.   Since starting his role last Friday, Miller has moved to reshape the administration’s policymaking process. He has organized a marathon series of meetings with cabinet secretaries and senior advisers to the president. He began gearing up for a confrontation with Democrats on Capitol Hill, who are preparing to launch dozens of investigations into the administration. And he has already had to navigate a crisis, as an international espionage scandal widens, pitting two of President Trump’s cabinet secretaries against each other. With Miller leading the West Wing, the Trump administration appears to be headed for a consequential and combative final chapter , report Meridith McGraw, Philip Wegmann and Alex Leary.

   5.   What Greece learned from going broke—and others in Europe still haven’t.   The dramatic protests that recently took place in Paris, Milan and other European cities over soaring living costs and deteriorating public services looked a lot like Athens circa 2010. Much has changed since then. The Greek economy is growing faster than the European Union average, albeit from a depressed level. At a time of widening deficits and ballooning public debts, the Greek government is one of the few in the West collecting more money than it spends. It is a remarkable turnaround that required a complete rethinking of the state’s approach to public finances. It also required a cultural reckoning, report Margherita Stancati and Yannis Palaiologos. Greeks, for better or worse, have learned to expect less from the state than many of their European peers.

In 2005, the NBA established that players must turn 19 the year of a given draft to qualify for selection. The “one-and-done” rule produced dozens of prospects who stopped on campus for exactly one season. But this season, three of the best teams in the sport—Duke, UCLA and Texas—have signed star recruits who ended their youth careers earlier than usual to join college rosters.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

• Shares of Nvidia closed the week down 13%. Despite the selloff extending to other chip makers Friday, the PHLX Semiconductor index, which includes Nvidia rivals such as AMD and Broadcom, logged a weekly gain of 8%.

Inside Stephen Miller’s frenetic first week as White House chief of staff.

5.

 

What Greece learned from going broke—and others in Europe still haven’t.

Much has changed since then. The Greek economy is growing faster than the European Union average, albeit from a depressed level. At a time of widening deficits and ballooning public debts, the Greek government is one of the few in the West collecting more money than it spends. It is a remarkable turnaround that required a complete rethinking of the state’s approach to public finances. It also required a cultural reckoning, report Margherita Stancati and Yannis Palaiologos. Greeks, for better or worse, have learned to expect less from the state than many of their European peers.

Unstoppable prison gangs are transforming Ecuador into a narco state.

Criminal organizations use Ecuador’s prisons as command centers for operations far beyond their concrete walls, authorities say. From inside jail cells, gangs have turned the country into a critical artery in the global cocaine trade. Once one of Latin America’s most peaceful nations, Ecuador is now among its most dangerous. The quest to find the crispest apple in America.
